title: Satellite Mission Planning with Rydberg Atoms
authors: Michel Nowak, Benjamin Marchand, Yassine Naghmouchi, Serge Rainjonneau, Wesley Coelho, Louis Vignoli, Louis-Paul Henry
abstract: Quantum computers relying on cold atoms are being built and promise a high flexibility in the way information in encoded into the physical system. In particular, the analog mode is spiking interest in the field of optimization as a classically intractable number of configurations can be tackled. In this work, we investigate a problem that requires every-day scheduling of critical tasks involving a large number of actors. Namely, fixing the planning for a Earth Observation satellite fleet composed of several of units exposed to a high density of targets to be scanned. We explore numerical schemes that convert the formulated problem into a cold-atoms friendly setup. We begin by a naive formulation of the Satellite Mission Planning problem without taking account for the agility of the satellites. We then extend the problem to take it into account based on the literature. By formulating the planning problem as a Maximum Independent Set problem, we are able to solve the problem with a QPU based on Rydberg atoms. We explore two ways of solving the MIS problem on the QPU, one relying on the graphs and on the Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization Framework (QUBO). We show that the QUBO methodology is the most relevant and explore it more deeply with numerical experiments. We conclude on the potential utility of using a QPU to solve the Satellite Mission Planning problem in an operational context.
summary: The paper tackles the complex scheduling challenge of Earth Observation satellites by reformulating it as a Maximum Independent Set problem. This problem is then mapped onto a Quantum Processing Unit built with Rydberg atoms, utilizing the QUBO framework for solution. The research validates the potential utility of this quantum approach for solving practical optimization tasks in space mission planning.
main_problem: The paper addresses Satellite Mission Planning, which is formulated as a complex scheduling optimization problem requiring maximizing completed observation requests under various physical constraints.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that the problem can be mapped to a Maximum Independent Set (MIS) solvable on a QPU based on Rydberg atoms using the QUBO framework. While current time-to-solution is slower than classical methods, the approach shows potential for future speedup.
method: The core method involves formulating the scheduling constraints into an MIS problem and then mapping this graph problem onto the hardware constraints of a Rydberg atom QPU via the Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) framework.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a Quantum Processing Unit (QPU) utilizing neutral Rydberg atoms, whose dynamics are modeled by an Ising Hamiltonian. The optimization is solved by minimizing the energy corresponding to the QUBO formulation of the MIS problem.
key_observables: Total number of completed observation requests (Global Satisfaction Rate), Time to Solution, and adherence to physical constraints like energy consumption and slew time.
important_parameters: The QPU size limit ($\sim 100$ nodes for subgraphs) dictates the need for decomposition routines; the comparison is made against classical solvers using various time discretization steps ($\Delta T$).
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include simplifying power consumption models and assuming that future hardware enhancements will overcome current time-to-solution overheads compared to classical methods.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the problem setup (satellite trajectories), the MIS formulation using different methods (EDGES/AGILE), the QUBO solving process, and benchmark plots comparing completion rates and solution times between quantum and classical solvers as the number of requests increases.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the complex Satellite Mission Planning problem to formulating it mathematically as an MIS. It then details mapping this to a QUBO solvable on Rydberg atoms, presenting comparative benchmarks against state-of-the-art classical algorithms, and concluding with feasibility analysis for operational use.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant because it applies advanced quantum simulation techniques (Ising/QUBO models) from AMO physics—specifically using Rydberg atom platforms—to solve a large-scale combinatorial optimization problem derived from real-world engineering challenges.
